Header:

- Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Redwood SRE), Jules Carter (Redwood Solutions); Sarah Nguyen (EdgeScale ML infra lead), Diego Marconi (EdgeScale Platform), Priya Rao (EdgeScale SRE), Liam O'Connor (EdgeScale PM)

Summary (auto):
Redwood and EdgeScale compare GPU runtime behavior between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM for an on-prem/NVLINK-enabled pilot. Focus on cold-start handoff, KV cache priming strategies, CUDA graph warm/replay stability, and how quantization/packing affects kernel selection and latency P99. Discuss tradeoffs for multi-tenant VPC-like deployment vs dedicated on-prem reservation. Agreed to exchange traces and run a targeted micro-bench.

Topics (auto):
- KV priming vs prefetching
- CUDA graph replay instability and replay jitter
- Kernel handoff heuristics (TRT-optimized kernels vs vLLM dynamic paths)
- Effect of int8 quantization on kernel selection and fallback
- VPC/on-prem network and KMS concerns

Action items (auto):
- See action_items metadata above.
- Links referenced: short deck: https://rwood.ai/decks/esl-kv-priming (redwood link, placeholder), microbench spreadsheet: https://rwood.ai/sheets/esl-kv-bench (redwood link)

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Alex Kim (Redwood): okay thanks everyone for joining, uh we'll try to keep this tight, we have about an hour, um, the goal is to walk through the microbenchmarks we ran on TRT-LLM and vLLM and then figure out the cold-start handoff story for your on-prem NVLINK nodes.
[00:00:15] Sarah (EdgeScale): great, and we, uh, we appreciate you doing the deep dive, last time we saw 2x variance at P99 depending on warmup, so hoping to pin that down.
[00:00:28] Priya Raman (Redwood): quick intro, I'm Priya SE, I ran the kernel traces and I have the nvprof/sim logs. there's a couple of surprising patterns — sometimes TRT-LLM picks a fused matmul kernel and other times vLLM triggers the dynamic aten path, which leads to different memory footprints and then cuda-graph replay behaves differently.
[00:00:45] Diego (EdgeScale): when you say fused matmul, that's the TRT custom kernel, right? not just the tensorrt conv?
[00:00:52] Priya: yeah fused matmul — it's the TensorRT-LLM path where it replaces attention+ffn with a fused kernel, lower launch overhead. but it has stricter memory alignment and priming needs. if the KV cache isn't primed with a few prefix tokens the allocator yields a different scratch layout and then cuGraph replay sometimes misses the right buffer addresses.
[00:01:12] Sarah: hmm we do prefix priming in our app for context pooling but not consistently; sometimes front-end strips prefixes for privacy reasons.
[00:01:22] Alex: that's common — so two levers: ensure prefix gets to the inference layer, or implement a deterministic priming step (cheap tokens) at route entry. both affect latency/cost.
[00:01:34] [00:01:34] Liam (EdgeScale): question on the warm path: if we do priming, does that meaningfully increase tokens billed or is there a cache that makes it free?
[00:01:42] Priya: good Q, depends on where you charge. Redwood hosted counts tokens, but if you're on-prem you control metering. operationally priming a short 8–16 token prefix usually pays back by removing jitter and reducing P99 tail, so net cost often drops for heavy tail workloads.
[00:01:58] Marcus Li (Redwood SRE): we saw a case where a 12-token priming reduced P99 by ~30% in our bench because it avoided a kernel fallback mid-stream.
[00:02:08] [00:02:08] Sarah: can you explain the fallback — what's the exact trigger?
[00:02:12] Priya: sure — in our traces fallback occurs when the runtime detects a memory layout mismatch or when a quantized kernel can't satisfy precision constraints for a particular head size; the runtime then switches to a generic aten path which is slower and can't be captured well by a cuGraph replay, so you get cudaGraph replay failures or replays with different buffer shapes, causing stalls.
[00:02:34] Diego: so quantization can cause fallback? we were planning int8 to save cost on our dedicated cluster.
[00:02:40] Priya: yes int8 helps but it's more brittle. TRT-LLM int8 fused kernels are fast but require calibration and consistent per-layer scaling. if a prompt causes dynamic range spikes, the kernel will fail an accuracy guard and switch to a patch path. vLLM's dynamic path handles range variability better but has higher per-token overhead.
[00:02:59] [00:02:59] Alex: think of it as: TRT-LLM gives you best steady-state throughput if you can keep the input distribution stable; vLLM is more forgiving but costlier at scale unless you tune batching aggressively.
[00:03:13] Sarah: can you show the nvprof snippet where the swap happens?
[00:03:18] Priya: yes, I pasted a short excerpt in the microbench sheet — on line 42 you'll see a kernel named tml_fused_attention_float32 and then later aten_matmul fallback at time 00:23:15 where memory pages were reallocated. the replay id changed which is the red flag.
[00:03:34] [00:03:34] Diego: that replay id change, is that deterministic to reproduce? we struggled to get it locally.
[00:03:39] Priya: it's not always deterministic; it's sensitive to concurrency and initial heap layout. small differences in earlier requests can shift addresses. we suspect allocator nondeterminism on certain driver versions. we reproduced more reliably when we forced identical startup sequences and disabled background SRE tasks.
[00:03:58] Marcus: note — driver version was 535.86 in our lab run; older drivers had slightly different behavior. we can share exact docker diff.
[00:04:07] [00:04:07] Liam: about CUDA graph replay — we saw intermittent replay fails during burst traffic, what would you recommend?
[00:04:14] Priya: two mitigations: deterministic priming + preallocated scratch pools. for on-prem you can reserve larger static buffers so cudaGraph replays always address the same offsets. Redwood's runtime can optionally pin a scratch pool per worker. that trades memory for stability.
[00:04:33] Sarah: what's the memory cost ballpark? we have 4x A100 80GB with NVLINK, but multi-tenant means we can't throw memory at everything.
[00:04:42] Priya: depends on model size — for a 13B model you'd reserve maybe 6–10GB per worker for scratch; for 70B it's more. We often recommend starting with a 10% basket for scratch, measure, then tune.
[00:04:56] [00:04:56] Diego: switching topics — kernel selection heuristics. how does I/O length distribution affect the choice?
[00:05:02] Priya: runtime uses a cost model that takes sequence length, batch distribution, quantization flags, and memory pressure. short sequences often prefer fused kernels because they reduce launch overhead; longer sequences may prefer unrolled aten ops to reuse memory. unexpected long tails in prompt length confuse the heuristic and cause path flips. you can configure the tiebreaker to prefer stable paths (we call it path_fidelity override).
[00:05:27] Sarah: hmm can we pin a path per model version? we want predictable latency for SLAs.
[00:05:31] Alex: yes you can pin a model to a runtime profile: prefer_trt, prefer_atten, or conservative. that is part of the rollout config we can share.
[00:05:40] [00:05:40] Priya: also worth mentioning batch packing: if you pack variable-length requests aggressively you can increase throughput but you may amplify eviction-induced fallbacks because the KV cache gets fragmented. so for multi-tenant vpc you might prefer conservative packing.
[00:05:58] Diego: packing vs batching — do you have heuristics for mixing them?
[00:06:02] Priya: yes, heuristics consider latency SLOs and tail percentiles. we use dynamic packing with an eviction-aware window: it packs requests only if the KV cache pressure is under threshold; otherwise it does per-request scheduling. that reduces kernel switching.
[00:06:18] [00:06:18] Marcus: we demonstrated in the microbench that enabling eviction-aware packing reduced kernel handoffs by 60% at the cost of ~6% throughput.
[00:06:26] Sarah: interesting — we care about P99, not raw throughput. that seems acceptable.
[00:06:31] [00:06:31] Priya: on quantization again — try hybrid: quantize FFN to int8 but keep attention in fp16. that lowers memory and keeps attention numerics stable which reduces triggers for fallback. TRT-LLM has a hybrid mode we tested.
[00:06:47] Diego: any pitfalls with hybrid? accuracy regressions?
[00:06:50] Priya: minimal if you calibrate. main pitfall is per-layer scaling drift with dynamic inputs; you should add a periodic calibration job or keep an outlier handling path.
[00:07:01] [00:07:01] Sarah: VPC and KMS question — if we run private on-prem with KMS, do you support HSM integrations?
[00:07:07] Alex: yes Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations via our connector. we can provide compliance docs. Marcus will follow up with required artifacts.
[00:07:18] [00:07:18] Marcus: I'll attach the KMS integration guide and the audit log sample.
[00:07:22] Priya: quick aside — network jitter can look like kernel fallback in traces because retransmits add delay; ensure your network metrics align when you see sudden P99 spikes.
[00:07:33] Diego: good point — we run over a segmented VPC with a NAT and we suspect occasional SNAT exhaustion. we'll add telemetry.
[00:07:40] [00:07:40] Liam: back to reproducibility — can Redwood run the same microbench in your lab to compare?
[00:07:45] Alex: yes, we'll run with your sample traces. please send token distribution and a request sample; we'll replay in our lab with identical driver, cuda, and docker image.
[00:07:55] Sarah: action item noted.
[00:07:58] [00:07:58] Priya: also saw one weirdness: when using CUDA Graphs with dynamic KV cache growth, some driver versions, I mentioned earlier, allocate new registration for each pattern which increases the launch time until the driver compacts. it's subtle.
[00:08:12] Diego: sounds like a defragmentation issue. any mitigation besides driver upgrade?
[00:08:16] Priya: two options: deterministic allocation at worker bootstrap or periodic worker recycle. we prefer deterministic allocation for production. worker recycle is easier but causes short disruptions.
[00:08:27] [00:08:27] Sarah: what's Redwood's recommended worker lifecycle?
[00:08:30] Alex: typically 24–72 hours with rolling restarts if you do worker recycle; for our Dedicated offering we do rolling restarts during low traffic windows. for on-prem you can choose pinned workers with deterministic alloc.
[00:08:42] [00:08:42] Marcus: one more datapoint — we measured guard-band thresholds: when memory pressure crosses 75% we switch kernels proactively to avoid fallback; that reduced fallback events by 45%.
[00:08:55] Diego: ok that helps.
[00:08:58] [00:08:58] Priya: final note — we observed a case where mixed-tenant load (small chat plus long context generation) caused kernel oscillation. mitigation is to route different workload classes to separate pools or tune the path_fidelity per route.
[00:09:16] Sarah: we currently have a single pool, so we'll scope route separation in the pilot.
[00:09:22] [00:09:22] Alex: wrapping up — recap and next steps: Redwood to share annotated traces and the microbench sheet; EdgeScale to send request traces and sample workloads; Redwood will propose pilot plan including driver/docker versions and a canary rollout with pinned path. schedule on-prem smoke test week of 2026-06-08.
[00:09:42] Priya: one last thing — I'll include a short script to prime the KV cache deterministically (8 tokens) and scripts to dump replay ids for debugging.
[00:09:53] Sarah: perfect, thanks.
[00:09:55] [00:09:55] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links and action items.
[00:10:00] [crosstalk, some overlap] Diego: thanks - bye.
